decision: The release summary starts with three auditable facts, then every improvement links to its working proof
why: A reviewer should understand the scope in seconds and verify any claim without hunting through navigation.
alternative: A prose release note with no deep links.
value: The page is both an executive summary and a fast reviewer itinerary.

decision: Twelve numbered cards use one repeated hierarchy: tags, change, reviewer value and proof link
why: The prompt has twelve equally important themes; a stable reading rhythm makes a dense release scannable.
value: Design, UX, architecture, engineering and cost can be compared at a glance.

decision: The living-world card points to the same deterministic browser simulation used by every zone
why: One event source keeps screens, traces, chaos and screenshots consistent without server infrastructure.
alternative: Independent timers and fixtures per application.
value: The systems visibly agree, work offline and cost $0 to operate.

decision: The pattern card names familiar interaction models while linking to a product with its own visual identity
why: Interaction literacy is useful; copying another company’s signature brand language is not.
alternative: Generic cards that hide the design references, or direct visual imitation.
value: Reviewers see broad consumer fluency and original art direction together.

decision: Free-tier constraints are presented as an architecture outcome, not a footnote
why: Static-first delivery, simulation and resource reuse materially shape the system and deserve the same scrutiny as scale choices.
alternative: Ignore operating cost in a portfolio demo.
value: The release remains sustainable on shared free accounts while still demonstrating depth.
